In horse racing, your payout will change based on the way the market moves to create the final odds. The final odds you'll be paid out at are determined by how much is bet on each horse and the Takeout.            The standard horse racing unit for win, place, or show bets is $2.                     Win           The win bet is simply betting on which horse will come in first place. Using the 2026 Herbie Dyke Stakes as an example, the winner was Legarto and finished with 12-5 odds. A $2 Win bet paid $6.80, a product of the standard $4.80 for a 12-5 payout on a $2 bet, plus your original $2 wager amount back.                      Place           The Place bet allows you to wager on whether a horse will finish first or second in a race, meaning two Place bets will pay out on each race. This gives you a greater chance of winning, but lowers your odds on the horse if they place.            Using the 2025 Kentucky Derby as the example again, a $2 Place bet on the No. 18 horse only returned $7.50 compared to the $17.96 for a Win bet. But also, a $2 Place bet on the No. 8 horse (Journalism), who was the favorite but came in second, paid $4.94 while the Win bet lost.                       Show           A Show bet is an even more conservative betting option. You are wagering on whether a horse will finish in the top three positions. That means three Show bets will pay out each race. For example, a $2 Show bet on a 10-1 winner returned $4. As one might expect, show bet odds are far less favorable than win bet odds, making them one of the more conservative wagers available in horse racing.                       Win/Place           You can also combine these bets on each horse when you're placing your wagers. That means if you want to bet on a horse to win and place, you can do that. A $2 Win/Place bet really means you're betting $4 – a $2 Win bet and a $2 Place bet. If the horse you bet on wins, you will win both bets. If the horse finishes second, you would only win the Place bet.                       Place/Show           The same is available for a Place/Show bet, where a $2 Place/Show bet would be $4 wagered on a $2 Place bet and a $2 Show bet. If your horse finishes first or second, you would win both, but if it finishes third, you would only win the Show bet.                       Win/Place/Show (Across The Board)            Lastly, you can bet on all three options in what is often referred to as an Across The Board bet. A $2 Across The Board bet would really be $6 wagered – $2 on Win, $2 on Place, and $2 on Show. If you make an Across The Board bet and your horse wins, you pay out on all three wagers.            It's important to note that betting on Win/Place/Show combinations may not result in a net return even if one of the bets pays. For example, at the 2024 Kentucky Derby, an Across The Board bet on the 11 horse would've returned just $5.58 on $6 wagered.                       The most popular horse racing bet types           Many horse racing bettors place exotic bets to try to predict where multiple horses will finish in a race. These combination wagers offer the chance for bigger payouts, but come with a lower probability of winning (just like same game parlays in sports betting).            It is important to note that, unlike sports betting, there is no standard odds calculation to use for determining exotic payouts. Because of parimutuel wagering, odds can fluctuate until the race begins based on which horses are taking the most action. Additionally, live horse racing betting is available to those interested, adding another layer of entertainment for those watching races as they take place.           Exactas           An exacta bet in horse racing functions the same as it does in other sports. The bettor must pick the exact finishing order. For example, if someone wants to place an exacta bet with two horses, they must select each horse and where it will finish exactly. Once again using the 2025 Kentucky Derby as an example, a $2 exacta on the No. 18 and No. 8 horses (who closed with final odds of 7-1 and almost 3-1) paid $48.32. This style of betting can be seen in plenty of other sports, especially in futures betting.Exotics winnings will vary based on the number of horses in the race, the odds of the top-finishing horses, and the size of the pool. For example, the field for the 2024 Kentucky Derby saw a longer shot horse win, so the exacta pool paid $258.56 -- significantly more than the 2025 Derby.                       Trifectas           This horse racing wager is placing a bet on the exact order of the top-three finishers in a race. A straight trifecta will pay handsomely, but is extremely difficult to hit. Trifecta payouts are often shown for $0.50 bets, but some will show for $1 bets as well. The payout screen will tell you which, but that's important to note so you're aware of how much you are getting back.            The 2025 Kentucky Derby Trifecta paid $231.12 on a $1 Trifecta bet.                       Superfectas           Superfecta bets try to predict the exact order of the top-four finishers in a horse race. The superfecta payout is usually shown for a $1 bet. For the 2025 Kentucky Derby, a $1 superfecta that added the fourth-place No. 3 horse to the trifecta paid $1,682.27.                      Super High 5           Some books will even allow you to bet on the top-five finishers in their exact order in what is called a Super High 5 bet. Those payouts will again be shown for a $1 wager. The odds of hitting a Super High 5, especially in a large field race, are exceptionally low. They are equivalent to multi-leg futures parlays in sports betting.The 2025 Kentucky Derby's $1 Super High Five paid $38,405.96.                      Box           A box bet allows you to have every possible combination for exotics. If you think you know which two horses will hit the exacta but are not sure of their specific order, you can box it. The same goes for trifectas and superfectas. The more horses you box together, the lower your total profits on the payout will be.            For example, a three-horse exacta box bet costs $12 to bet, as you are betting $2 on all six potential combinations between those three horses:           $2 on No. 1 in first, No. 2 in second$2 on No. 2 in first and No. 3 second$2 on No. 3 in first and No. 1 in second$2 on No. 3 in first and No. 2 in second$2 on No. 2 in first and No. 1 in second$2 on No. 1 in first and No. 3 in secondYou can do the same for Trifectas and Superfectas, but at exponentially escalating costs. A $1 Trifecta Box with three horses is six combinations, so $6 wagered:           $1 on No. 1 in first, No. 2 in second, No. 3 in third$1 on No. 1 in first, No. 3 in second, No. 2 in first$1 on No. 2 in first, No. 1 in second, No. 3 in third$1 on No. 2 in first, No. 3 in first, No. 1 in second$1 on No. 3 in first, No. 1 in second, No. 2 in third$1 on No. 3 in first, No. 2 in second, No. 1 in firstFrom there, four horses in a $1 trifecta box is 24 combinations for $24 wagered. Five horses is 60 possible combinations for $60.            A $1 Superfecta box of four horses is $24 wagered, five horses is $120 wagered and six horses is $360 wagered.                       How to bet on horse racing: Multi-race wagers           While those exotics offer a variety of options for betting on individual races, you can also bet on multiple races at the same track in various ways. These combination wagers pay out based on the betting pool, allowing you to choose a handful of horses you're confident in throughout the day to increase your potential payout.                       Daily Double           The Daily Double is exactly what it sounds like: Betting on back-to-back race winners from that day. The odds for Daily Doubles vary based on the odds for the individual horses you bet and the overall Daily Double betting pool. As an example, the $2 Daily Double at Horseshoe Indianapolis on April 15, 2025 from the first two races with the 7 horse in the first race (went off at 1-1 odds) and the 4 horse in the second race (went off at 3-5 odds) paid $8.            Once the first race ends, the payouts for each potential Daily Double will be shown under a "Will Pays" tab on the next race's betting screen.                       Pick-3, Pick-4, Pick-5 and Pick-6           Along with the Daily Double, there are more options for betting the winner of multiple races in a row at the same track. The Pick-3 is picking the winner in three consecutive races, the Pick-4 in four consecutive races, and so on for the Pick-5 and Pick-6.           Like exotics, the pool amount and the odds for each horse wagered on determine the payouts for these multi-race wagers. The default unit for these bets varies from book to book, with FanDuel showing $0.50 payouts and TwinSpires showing $1 payouts in the Will Pays section.            The more races you put together on a ticket, the more you can win. But as with any multi-race wager, the more legs you add, the harder it is to win. In this way, these bets function similarly to parlays in other sports.For some of the biggest races, the Pick-6 will feature a set guaranteed prize pool for the winner(s) no matter what the actual wagered amount is. The 2024 Kentucky Derby featured a $1 million guaranteed pool on TwinSpires for Pick-6s on races 6 through 11 at Churchill Downs.                       Understanding horse racing payouts           After the race, the winning payouts will be displayed for each bet type. The standard unit for win/place/show and exactas is a $2 bet. Trifectas, superfectas and super high 5s are typically shown as $1 or $0.50, but will say explicitly which on the payout board.            The payouts for each horse in the top three for the 2025 Kentucky Derby looked as follows:           2025 Kentucky DerbyWinPlaceShowSovereignty (No. 18) 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$17.96 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$7.50 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$5.58 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Journalism (No. 8) 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 								           $4.94 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$3.70 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Baeza (No. 21) 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 								           				           $8.38 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				           If you bet more (or less) than the standard $2 unit, you multiply the payout by how much you bet and divide by the standard unit. For example, a $10 Win bet on Sovereignty returned $89.80, while a $25 Show bet on Journalism would've returned $46.25.            For the single-race exotics at the 2025 Kentucky Derby, the payouts were as follows:            2025 Kentucky DerbyPayout$2 Exacta (18-8) 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$48.32 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$1 Trifecta (18-8-21) 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$231.12 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$1 Superfecta (18-8-21-3) 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$1,682.27 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$1 Super High 5 (18-8-21-3-20) 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$38,405.96 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				          Biggest horse races beyond Kentucky Derby betting          The horse racing calendar operates year-round, but there are six events on the schedule that serve as the most important, thus attracting the best fields. The three Triple Crown events headline for the general public, but the Breeders' Cup, Pegasus World Cup and Dubai World Cup all offer massive purses and attract some of the best horses and fields in all of racing.           October 30-31, 2026: Breeders' Cup January 23, 2027: Pegasus World CupMarch 27, 2027: Dubai World CupMay 1, 2027: Kentucky DerbyMay 15, 2027: Preakness StakesJune 5, 2027: Belmont Stakes           Triple Crown of horse racing           The Kentucky Derby, Preakness Stakes and Belmont Stakes make up horse racing's Triple Crown. There are 13 horses that have completed the Triple Crown, winning all three events, and just two – American Pharoah (2015) and Justify (2018) – have accomplished that feat in the 21st century.            Not every horse competes in all three Triple Crown events. Each race operates at different lengths, and the turnaround time can be too quick for trainers to be comfortable running their horse in one after the other. Some Derby winners don't run the Preakness, while some have made it two legs before withdrawing from the Belmont.            The Kentucky Derby is a 1 1/4 mile race, the Preakness Stakes is 1 3/16 mile, and the Belmont Stakes is a grueling 1 1/2 mile event (although it is being run currently at 1 1/4 mile at Saratoga Race Course due to renovations at Belmont Park).                       Tips and advice for betting on horse racing           There are a number of strategies for betting on horse racing, but it all starts with understanding the horses and knowing their strengths, weaknesses and past performances.                       Racing forms and past performances           These are race-day publications and programs available at tracks and online to preview the day's races at each track. They are full of data and information from past races. All of the best horse racing betting apps have integrated much of this information into their betting screen.                       Track conditions           Before you even get to the horses, understanding track conditions is vital. Knowing if a track is dirt or grass, firm and fast or soft and slow, is critical information to know so you can look at which horses in a given race run best in certain conditions.                       Horse tendencies            From there, you want to understand the tendencies of horses in the field. Some horses get out to fast starts and try to push the pace, while others hang back and try to make a late kick. If most of the field is expected to push the pace and run it fast, then a horse that prefers to stay back may be at an advantage due to an unsustainable early pace.            The opposite could be true, too; if the pace is going to be slower early, frontrunners are more likely to hold their position. Some of this information can be found in PPs or Past Performance data.                       Post position           Post position can also matter to a horse's success. Some prefer to run the rail (on the inside of the track) while others prefer being on the outside and having more space. This information is all worth considering and comparing with the other horses in the field.                      Trainer and jockey information           A horse's trainer and jockey will also have tendencies. Some trainers are better at getting horses ready for a certain type of track, but maybe don't have a great track record at others. Some jockeys may be more or less aggressive on the track, which may or may not work well with that specific horse's tendencies, or they may have a long track record with that horse and know how to get the most out of them.                       Workout times           There's also plenty of data available that can help you. Workout times, if available, can give you an idea of how a horse has been running in training before a big race.                       Speed figures           Speed figures are like advanced stats of the horse racing world, offering a metric to show how well a horse has been running in its recent races that factors in things like field strength and track quality.            Taking all of that data into account is important to betting on horse racing, and for beginners it's best to ease in and do as much observing as you do betting. You'll start to find certain trends for horses, jockeys, trainers and tracks that can help you find edges on the odds board going forward.                      Manage your horse racing betting bankroll           Managing your bankroll with what percentage of money you have set aside for horse racing betting is vital to increasing your chances of scoring big at some point. Just like in sports betting, where most bankroll management experts advise no more than 2% of your bankroll should be bet on any given game, the same principle can be applied to any given horse race.                       Rules and responsible gaming           Responsible gambling is taken very seriously across all racebooks. All provide the necessary resources and contact information if you or someone you know may have a gambling problem. The minimum age is 18 for horse racing betting in most states, but it is 21 in some states.           Responsible gambling resources include the National Council for Problem Gambling (NCPG) and Gamblers Anonymous. Be smart. Bet smart. Wager responsibly. Those in need of help can also call or text 1-800-GAMBLER (1-800-426-2537). Help is available 24 hours a day and seven days a week.           FAQHow to bet on horse racing?There are several ways to bet on horse racing. The most common methods are through horse racing betting apps like TwinSpires, FanDuel Racing, and DraftKings Horse. Users can bet on a variety of outcomes, with the most common wager coming on which horse will win the given race outright.How to bet on horse racing online?Online horse racing betting is widely accessible. TwinSpires, DraftKings Horse, and FanDuel Racing all provide users with a huge array of betting options on all major races.What is a box bet in horse racing?A box bet in horse racing involves picking the finishing order of the horses. Wagerers can choose the order of the first two, three, four, or five finishers, with the return on their bet increasing with every additional horse they include in their wager. If a bettor chooses three horses for a box bet, they do not need to finish in an exact order. If they make up the top three, the bet is successful.What is a show bet in horse racing?A show bet is a wager on a specific horse to finish among the top three horses in a given race. Show bets are extremely common wagers that offer less risk and smaller payouts.What is a key box bet in horse racing?A key box bet, unsurprisingly, functions similarly to a box bet. A bettor can select a "key" horse that they believe will finish in an exact position while rounding out the rest of the box in the same fashion as a regular box bet. For example, a bettor could select Horse A to finish first while picking Horses C, B, and D to round out the top four. However, if Horse A does not finish first, the bet loses.

title: Inside the fastest show in baseball: What it's like to watch Brewers sensation Jacob Misiorowski - CBS Sports

body:
MILWAUKEE – The greatest show on the sand, silt, and clay of the pitcher's mound these days is Milwaukee Brewers right-handed force of nature Jacob Misiorowski. The 24-year-old is not just the best pitcher in the world in 2026, he's also the most viscerally overwhelming pitcher in the world. Misiorowski on Friday at the Brewers' home yard squared off against Chris Sale, one of the best at his craft and a pitcher some 13 years Misiorowski's senior. It was not only a clash of aces, it was also a duel between two of the best teams in baseball. The 40,130 in attendance -- marking the 16th Milwaukee sell-out of the season (and this one on weekday afternoon) – surely knew it meant a little more than most August games do.  Beyond the importance of the outcome -- Milwaukee won 2-1 -- and what it meant to a Brewers team trying to fend off the Cubs and secure top seed throughout the postseason and a Braves team angling to secure a bye, it was a Misiorowski start. No matter the opponent, that's appointment viewing these days. If you were watching, here's what you saw. First inningWorking from the first base side of the rubber, Misiorowski opens with a 101.8 mph fastball to greet Braves leadoff hitter Ronald Acuña Jr. It's a ball inside. Misiorowski will go to the fastball with all five pitches that Acuña sees -- all triple digits, and four of them out of the zone. Acuña flicks away the only strike, one on the outside sliver of the zone, and works a walk. 
With most starting pitchers, we'd note that they'd now be working from the stretch. Misirowski, though, is unusual among starting pitchers in that he always works from the stretch. Perhaps, with his long levers and maxed-out stuff, keeping it simple is the soundest approach. It's certainly impossible to argue with the results, just as it's impossible to argue with the Brewers' faculties when it comes to pitching development. On Misiorowski's sixth pitch of the game, he finally departs from the fastball and presents Drake Baldwin with a 98-mph cutter. Two offerings later, he goes to the slider for the first time on Friday. It's not his fully gassed-up slider. He's touched 98 with his slider this season, although when his slide-piece is at those levels, it might be more of a cutter than a true slider. If you call it a true slider, then Misiorowski has thrown 49 of the 50 fastest sliders on record. Is a 98-mph slider more impressive than his occasional 104-mph fastball? It might be, if, of course, it's a slider in the genuine sense and not a cutter or the infelicitously named slutter. We know that his fastball is a fastball, though, so it's fine to direct your amazement there, as you likely already were. Misiorowski gets his first strikeout of the game on a 101.6 mph fastball that catches the outside edge at Baldwin's expense. 
Speaking of the typical purpose of pitching from the stretch -- to hold runners -- preventing the steal is a skill of Misiorowski's that gets overlooked. On that note: This was a delayed steal on the part of Acuña, so the out was more an instance of poor decision-making running headlong into William Contreras' powerful throwing arm. Contreras is among the game's best when it comes to controlling the running game, but let's note that Misiorowski has allowed only one stolen base this season – the fewest among qualifiers alongside Ryan Weathers.  Not long after, Misiorowski ends the frame with a backfoot slider to Matt Olson that he whiffs on. He throws the slider about three times as often to right-handed batters, but, as Olson will surely attest, he can back-foot it to left-handed batters as a putaway pitch. This one was 91.8 mph, so, yes, it's a true slider. 
Second inningIt seems like the merest matter of time before Misiorowski eventually authors a no-hitter, but it won't be today. With two out, Mauricio Dubón lines an 0-2 fastball to right for a single. At 103.1 mph, the pitch is Misiorowski's hastiest of the day and the first pitch we've seen enter what's informally known as "Miz Velo Country." It's not particularly fair to throw that hard as a starting pitcher, and what makes it even less fair from the Misiorowski standpoint is how close to the plate he releases the ball. The 6-foot-7 Misiorowski gets, on average, an absurd 7.6 feet of extension off the rubber and toward the plate. That puts him in the 99th percentile in extension among big league hurlers. Take a look at Misiorowski's first inning landing spot, as amateurishly captured from the American Family Field press box: 
And here's how it looked in the fourth inning after Sale has put his spikes on the mound: As you can see, the 6-foot-6 Sale had been planting well behind Misirowski. Sale gets his six-and-a-half feet in extension, on average, and that puts him in the 59th percentile, but thanks to his crossfire delivery he doesn't get down the hill as much as Misiorowski does. That's where the notion of effective velocity comes into play. The hitter obviously has vanishingly little time to react to Misiorowski's fastball, and because he releases the ball so close to the hitter, it's even less time than you might think. Misiorowski this season has averaged 100.6 mph with his fastball, but his average effective velocity -- meaning what the pitch feels like to the hitter -- is 103.1 mph thanks to his elite extension. He has a high leg lift, with the knee basically coming in line with the jersey lettering when he's going into his delivery, and that sets him up to stride deep toward the plate. 
When we talk about Miz's fastball, we'll often couch it in terms like "fastest by a starting pitcher" when talking about Aroldis Chapman in historical terms or Mason Miller on the contemporary front. Miller indeed does best Misiorowski on the radar gun, with an average four-seamer of 101.5 mph. In effective velocity, though, Miller comes in at 102.4 mph because he gets less extension than Misiorowski. Miller may throw harder, but most hitters would probably tell you that Miz seems like he throws hardest of all.  He induced a 2-1 fly-out from Dom Smith to strand Dubón and end the inning. Third inningThe third frame, in which after the first two batters Misiorowski gets into the Atlanta lineup for the second time, sees him take a slider-heavy approach. Of his 11 pitches in the inning, just three are fastballs. He goes to the four-seamer more than 60% of the time overall, which is a point of distinction these days, so this is a brief departure for Misiorowski. Like most teams, the Braves are less effective against breaking stuff than fastballs, and Misiorowski is getting deeper into his secondaries a bit early, since he probably won't go extremely deep into this game even if the zeroes continue to stack up. He's pitching on extra rest, as is custom with him lately, as his workload continues to mount and as the Brewers increasingly operate with a focus on a deep October run. Misiorowski whiffs Austin Riley on a fastball after feeding him three straight sliders. Against the Braves No. 9 hitter, Mike Yastrzemski, he throws a curve for the first time. The curve is actually Miz's best pitch in terms of whiff rate, but this one lands a bit too middle-in, and Yastrzemski lines it to right for a single. First pitch ground-outs to Acuña and Baldwin end the frame. 
Fourth inningFreshly staked to a 2-0 lead, Misirowski benefits from the first ABS challenge of the day by Contreras, who flips a called ball into a called strike at the top of the zone to put Olson in an 0-1 count. He's back to a fastball-heavy approach in this inning and throws three straight balls to Olson before retiring him on back-to-back swinging strikes at the fastball. With a 2-1 count, Harris stings a 99.7 mph high fastball – it's the first hard-hit ball that Misiorowski has permitted on this day – but center fielder Luis Lara makes a nifty ranging catch to prevent extra bases. The 16-pitch perfect frame ends on an Ozzie Albies fly-out. Fifth inningFor a pitcher like Misiorowski, who doesn't throw a sinker and leans so heavily on a four-seamer he likes to spot high in the zone, you wouldn't expect strong groundball tendencies. But Misiorowski has a ground-ball percentage of 45.1, which puts him in the 64th percentile among MLB hurlers. This is because his secondaries all get more grounders than you'd expect given their traits and types. The fifth provides a reminder, and Dubón leads off the inning by grounding out to Brice Turang at second on a Miz cutter. The pitch was at the very top of the zone, but because of the late natural sink it dipped under the barrel and registered a -3 degree launch angle. Another ground ball followed, but this one off the bat of Smith (with a -17 degree launch angle) sneaked into right field for a hit. Facing Riley for the second time, Misiorowski flipped his approach and went fastballs broken up by a slider. He earned a whiff. The Braves brought the potential tying run to the plate when Yastrzemski earned a four-pitch walk -- not a common occurrence for Misiorowski. Yes, his stuff is electricity set on fire, but it's all harnessed and commanded. He's walked just 6% of opposing batters, which is figure that puts him among the league's top control artists (a descriptor that, even so, will never be applied to him). This walk meant Misiorowski would face the perilous Acuña for the third time on Friday in a crucial spot. With a 1-2 count, he fed the former MVP a fastball above the zone followed by a slider at the very bottom of it. One -17 degree launch angle later, a 6-3 putout ended the threat. 
Sixth inningImprobably, Misiorowski this season has permitted a .122/.230/.194 line when facing an opposing lineup for the third time in a start. Still, in-game familiarity benefits the hitter, and the theory holds even when a pitcher like Misiorowski is defying it. The sixth indeed occasioned danger for the Milwaukee ace. To start, he freezes Baldwin for a punchout on the sixth pitch of their encounter. Next was Olson, and Misiorowski got ahead 0-2 thanks to two different brands of sliders – one back door and one back foot. Olson evens the count at 2-2 and then bruises a high fastball, 104.8 mph off the bat, to center. Lara, though, is on the case: The ball off Olson's bat had an expected batting average of .770, but in truth that figure turned out to be .000. Two pitches later, Harris smoked a double to right off a slider, and a mound visit followed. An Albies fly-out put an end to the inning. With a pitch count of 96 Misiorowski's day was probably already done, but the Brewers no doubt noted that against Albies he threw his slowest four-seamer at 97.2 mph and his slowest cutter at 94.7 mph. The Fatigued state is when mechanics go awry, and we know what can happen from there. Wielding the beast of unthinkable velocity means respecting it, at least if you want to keep wielding it. He wasn't his sharpest self in that inning, and, who can say, if the sunlight didn't break through that bank of windows at American Family Field in the sixth and complicate the hitting visuals, maybe it's not a spotless day after all for Misiorowski. 
His final line: 
As of that work, Misiorowski this season has an ERA of 1.68 and an FIP of 2.14 in 145 innings. He's also struck out 216 batters, which comes to a K% of 39.3 -- an absurd figure for any pitcher, let alone a starter who isn't even a quarter-century old yet. All of that -- everything, really -- leads the majors.   The Braves broke through against the Milwaukee bullpen with a run in the eighth and put the tying run on base in the ninth, but in the end the crisp two-hour and 21-minute pitcher's duel -- connoisseur's baseball -- went the way most expected it to. It went to the better team and -- this is often said in reference to a probable future Hall of Famer like Sale -- the better pitcher. The Brewers, thanks to the heavy lifting of Misiorowski, are now the first team to 80 wins in 2026. Given the two moundsmen involved and the two teams involved, it all felt like a prelude to something bigger, say, seven or eight weeks from now. That sounds all right, does it not?
